posts.title: How we make money (and why it matters to you)
posts.body:
Every analytics tool makes money somehow. If you can't tell how, it's worth asking.

Here's how Plausible makes money: site owners pay us a subscription. That's the whole model.

We're independent. We're self-funded. We're profitable. We're based in the EU. And we don't sell customer data.

That last point isn't a line in a policy we could quietly rewrite later. It's how the business works. Our revenue comes from over 21,000 paying subscribers, not from what their visitors do.

Why this should matter to you:
→ When a tool is free, it's fair to ask what pays for it.
→ When you pay, you're the customer. Our incentives line up with yours.
→ There's no outside investor waiting for us to find a new revenue stream in your data.

Plausible isn't free, and it isn't the right fit for every analytics use case. We'd rather say that up front.

But if you want clear website stats and a straight answer about where the data goes, it's worth a look.

posts.title: No cookies in analytics means one less reason for a cookie banner
posts.body:
A cookie banner on every page of your site, just so your analytics can count visits. That's a lot of friction for a page-view number.

Plausible doesn't use cookies and doesn't collect personal data. Nothing personal is stored on the visitor's device and nothing personal is collected, so there's no GDPR consent form to show for analytics.

That changes two things for a site owner. Visitors land on your page instead of a pop-up. And people who would have clicked "reject" still get counted, because there's nothing for them to reject.

One honest limit. If your site also loads ad pixels, chat widgets or embedded videos that set cookies, those still need consent. Cookie-free analytics takes one item off the banner. Whether the banner goes away depends on everything else you load.

So before you change any tool, open your site in a private window and check which cookies are set before anyone clicks anything. Write down what each one is for. If analytics is the only reason your banner exists, that's the first thing to change.

posts.title: The analytics script is the one script every visitor loads
posts.body:
Your analytics script loads on every page, for every visitor, on every connection. Plausible's is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics.

That matters because analytics is the one script you never skip. A large hero image only loads on the homepage. The tracking script runs everywhere, including on the phone of someone on a train with one bar of signal.

We kept ours small by keeping it to its job: counting visits without cookies and without collecting personal data. Less code to download means less for the browser to fetch and run before your page is done.

You can check what your current setup costs in a couple of minutes. Open your site in Chrome, open DevTools, go to the Network tab and reload the page. Filter by your analytics provider's domain and look at the transfer size of every request it makes, then compare that with the size of your logo.

If your analytics outweighs your logo, you've found a speed fix that needs no redesign and no new hosting.

What's the heaviest script on your site that nobody on the team remembers adding?
